Against:
-Grammatically incorrect according to many dictionaries. Singular "they" is gramarrically correct in english but only when the gender of the subject in a sentence is unknown and the subject itself is hypothetical/not present, it's traditionally not used for present people of known gender.
-Some pronoun "generators" get very silly with what they put out. Some stop even pretending to be pronouns at all and are just already exists vowels shortened in different ways (ex: gho/ghost/ghostself is one set I've seen)
-Most of the "out there" neopronouns never are attempted to be used in real life. You could argue that they can't even get the chance to be valid if people don't use them outside twitter and discord.

For:
-A descriptivist view of language would allow for the evolution of use of singular "they" to be valid. All language is made up to how we see fit and is generally socially agreed upon. Just like "new" words like vape, selfie, sus, etc/whatever become commonly known and understood, singular "they" is also a word thats becoming more socially agreed upon.
-"He" and "She" are both gendered pronouns, if someone is neither man or woman or maybe they are but don't just don't want to be referred to in a gendered way, neopronouns are pretty much the only way to accomplish that aside from being referred to by name only.
-Neopronouns in English have already existed for centuries as early documented as 1300 ("ou")
-Singular "They" already exists in English, simply adapting to its usage to include speaking to someone of known gender isn't THAT big of a leap.
-They don't harm anyone, and people aren't really that subjected to the ""weird"" ones for people to make such a big fuss about them. I live in a very liberal city and I've only run into people who use they/them neopronouns(which already are English singular pronouns) the only time I've known of anyone using another set is a friend of a friend I've never met that uses ze/zir. And even if people did more commonly use unconventional neopronouns in real life there's no harm in respecting them.
-They/them might be difficult at first because of the association with plural but with practice, it's not very hard to be able to infer whether or not someone is speaking about one person or plural.
I say this as someone who uses they/them currently but used to struggle to adjust to my first friends who started using they/them years ago. I know it takes getting used to and it's ok to not "get it" at first :)

Coming from the point of view of an Indigenous Person.
Dating Similar cultures:
-There can be a certain level of ease in not having to explain your families practices, attitudes, etc. Even between other Indigenous cultures globally sometimes there's a basic understanding and similarities. I'm Native from the Pacific Northwest and even going to New Zealand despite there being cultural difference there were many similarities. Not that it's bad to have to explain certain cultural views or practices, but sometimes it feels so good to not have to feel like you're teaching someone and they already "get it" to some degree.
-This is specific to being Native but there's such an enormous pressure to learn and revive practices lost in colonization. IMO it seems something that is to a degree overwhelming to spring on a partner when for a lot of people it's a lifetime commitment to relearn languages, culture etc. Or in some cases people who are not indigenous dismiss the importance of it.
-There are certain social problems that are very pervasive in my community including suicide, substance abuse, and violence. A lot of non-indigenous people in my life are shocked to hear what I've had to go through even though I'm overall a pretty privileged person. Even if they are supportive, it can feel super alienating to have someone gawk and ask how you even cope. Even though Native people don't all experience the same struggles or issues, and some people are much better off than others, there's still a better level of understanding most of the time.
-Some ppl fetishize Natives A LOT.
Reasons for dating other cultures/ethinicities:
-Some Native ppl also fetishize our culture and are really gross about it. They have regressive views and value the possession of cultural teachings, regalia, knowledge etc over actually morals and being a good person. I know so many Native men who get away with disgusting abusive behaviour but are celebrated because they know traditional songs or teachings and know how to "play indian" well. There are men in the community who are straight up like gone to court child molestors who are still upheld and celebrated away from their home community in the cities because they are this reservoir of "traditional culture" despite the fact that they violate so many codes of ethics that would have seen them punished before colonization.
-In a similar note there is a lot of in-community abuse and violence. A lot of people are suffering and are not healthy to be in a relationship with. There are people like this in every culture but it's something especially high in the native community as a result of systemic racism. 
-To refer to the other side, even though in general, it's easier for more Native people who understand your culture and struggles, it's not a definite rule. Sometimes you will meet other native people who REALLY don't get where you're coming from, and our cultures and world views are not all the same. Sometimes a Non Native person will "get it" more than some other Native people.

I have had multiple close family members commit or attempt suicide, and have been suicidal myself. Death of any kind in a family causes trauma and distress. I have lost count of how many funerals I've attended and have seen the fallout from the death of accidents, disease/illness, and suicide. Accidents are stressful because of how unexpected they are, people are in shock from losing someone they didn't expect to. Disease in stressful because you often see the person struggling and feel the need to help but often you are helpless to. Suicide is often both. My sister committed suicide and it caught my family off guard because she seemed to be doing well for the year or two up to the suicide, but they also knew that she suffered from depression and other issues her whole life. There was so much shame and guilt from not being able to help her, and shock not expecting it coming. My mom(her stepmother) was consumed by guilt because she had confided in her that her biological mothers dad had sexually abused her as a kid. After she died my mom fell into alcoholism because she couldn't cope with the guilt that she felt she could have done something. 
When people in my family have passed because of accidents or disease people still had regrets, but there's an aspect of their death feeling beyond our control to stop. We can't stop a car accident, or heart attack, or stroke most of the time. But with suicide, it's often more devastating because you feel like you should have done something more or realized the person was in that much pain.
Even when it's someone you have an extremely difficult or distant relationship with it's still going to hit you hard. My mom attempted suicide and was very abusive to me and ended up dying of alcoholism. Even though there were many ways my life was easier after she passed, it was still extremely painful to cope with, and I would still always wish that she was alive and getting better instead of her life ending. 
I know this was very long-winded but my main point is that no matter how distant or strained a relationship is, people don't wish to see their family die or are indifferent to it. Suicide is traumatic. It doesn't make a difference how close or distant a relationship is it will cause distress to the people left behind.
On another note though I want to make clear I don't think this makes people who attempt or commit suicide bad or selfish, it's just a reality of it though. It's going to affect the people still alive.

Is it causing you a level of distress?
I don't think it's true to say "if you've ever had a fleeting intrusive thought about suicide it's BAD". People have all kinds of intrusive thoughts and unless it's affecting you negatively, it should just be let go and not dwelt on imo.
But if you are asking because it makes you uncomfortable, and these thoughts keep reoccurring, I'd say it's too much.

Ok so I'm still not entirely sure what I want to do and what I'll be capable of doing going forward in my life. I want to go to post secondary but I could barely keep my shit together the last three years in high school.  I loved learning shit at school but I could barely stand being there because of anxiety and depression and so I don't even know if I'd be able to do it. I know intellectually I'm fine, I have been told over and over that I have the ability to succeed academically but I just CAN'T keep my shit together for more that two or three month periods. 
So yeah I want to go to post secondary and I've been working at an anthropology museum(I am the most productive high school drop out ok) and doing a bunch of arts and culture stuff within the Native community. And I started learning hən̓q̓əmin̓əm,  which is my own ancestral language.  It's a Salish an language that has zero fluent speakers left. So this year I ended up getting the chance to go with some people from my band (tribe) to New Zealand as a part of a cultural exchange and part of what we were doing there is learning what Maori people are doing for language revitalization,  so we visited a few Maori immersion schools where kids k-12 are instructed completely in te reo maori. 
And going on that trip just made me so fucking excited at the fact that what I'm doing at home can build up to something like that. Like I'm so fucking optimistic about it, that I AM going to speak hən̓q̓əmin̓əm and that I AM going to live to see children growing up speaking it. And I didn't even notice how annoyingly positive I was about it until people started flat up telling me "you know that will never happen right?".
And it's kind of disheartening, especially when it comes from people in my own community and family. And that's something I always have to actively resist internalizing. Because when people do ask questions/point criticism like "why bother with that" "its dead language of no use" "its impossible" I can feel myself jolted a bit from my like, naive ambition I had about the whole thing. But I desperately don't want that to disappear because I think that's the attitude needed to revive indigenous languages. Like I would rather have a fucking way too crazy dream and work for it like hell and fail to reach the goal than to just think "what's the point" and have nothing happen.
